  NOTICE OF SPECIAL MEETING
  OF THE
  ALHAMBRA HOUSING AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
  CITIZEN ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  (Notice No. N2M20-78)

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that a special meeting of the Alhambra Housing and
Community Development Citizen Advisory (HCDA) Committee will be held on
Tuesday, June 16, 2020, commencing at 7:00 p.m.

  CORONAVIRUS (COVID-19) ADVISORY NOTICE

Consistent with Executive Orders No. N-29-20 and No. N-35-20 from the Executive
Department of the State of California and the County of Los Angeles Department of Public
Health Safer At Home Order, the Alhambra Housing and Community Development
Citizen Advisory Committee meeting will not be physically open to the public and the
meeting will take place via teleconference and video conference.

To watch and listen to the meeting: To maximize public safety while still maintaining
transparency and public access, members of the public can participate by using Zoom
Meeting as follows:

Enter Meeting ID: 852 4698 3659 and Password: 882287

Please Note: All members of the public calling or logging into the meeting will be muted
so that the meeting can proceed. For those wishing to speak on an agenda item, please
email Matthew Cuevas at mcuevas@cityofalhambra.org by 5:00 p.m. prior to the meeting
with the item number you wish to speak on and the phone number you will use when
calling or the name you will use when logging into the meeting. You should then call or
log into the meeting at least 5 minutes prior to its start time. Staff will unmute you and
announce you when it is your time to speak. You will have five minutes to speak, unless
that time is adjusted by the meeting Chair.

As an alternative you can email your comments to the Matthew Cuevas at
mcuevas@cityofalhambra.org by no later than 5:00 p.m. on June 16, 2020 to ensure there
 is sufficient time to print the emails prior to the beginning of the meeting. Comments will
then be read into the record, with a maximum allowance of 5 minutes per individual
comment, subject to the Chair’s discretion. If a comment is received after 5:00 p.m. but
before the conclusion of the meeting based upon its time stamp, the comment will still be
included as a part of the record of the meeting but will not be read into the record.

  SPECIAL MEETING
HOUSING AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT CITIZEN ADVISORY COMMITTEE
  TUESDAY, JUNE 16, 2020 AT 7:00 P.M.

1. ROLL CALL:
  Bill Vallejos, Chair  Mark Lee, Vice Chair
  Bonita Sharma-Ngan  Andrea Giese
  Marc Tousignant  Sasha Renée Pérez
  Maria Conchita Bañuelos  Yvette Cardenas
  Marcos Sayon

2. MINUTES
  Approval of the minutes for the Special Meeting of January 30, 2020.

3. PROGRESS REPORTS
  Attached for the Committee’s review are copies of the Progress Reports for those programs
  utilizing Community Development Block Grant and HOME Funds. All figures indicate the
  progress made and services rendered to date for FY 2019-2020.
   Parks and Recreation - Case Management
   96 Case Management clients were served.
   135 Volunteer Hours of assistance were donated to the program.
   Community Development - Code Enforcement
   The Code Enforcement Division investigated a total of 482 complaints.
   64 were identified as confirmed complaints as stand-alone Health & Safety Issues.
   Code Enforcement staff referred 152 to the Housing Department programs.
   Community Development - Fair Housing
   The Housing Rights Center served approx. 243 clients.
   A variety of issues were discussed, including: evictions, security deposits, rent
  increases, repairs, contract questions, etc.
   Community Development - Housing Programs
   First-Time Home Buyer - HOME: 10 searching for a home, 2 escrow closed.
   HOME Major Rehabilitation: 0 in process, 1 completed.
   CDBG Minor Rehabilitation: 0 in process, 1 completed.

  Recommended Action
  Receive and file these informational reports.

4. DRAFT 2020-2024 CONSOLIDATED PLAN AND 2020-2021 ANNUAL ACTION
  PLAN
  The Housing and Community Development Citizens Advisory Committee will conduct a
  public meeting to receive input on City programs funded with Housing and Urban
  Development Funds and the community’s need during fiscal years 2020-2024. Staff will
  provide an overview of the programs proposed for the next program year in the 2020-2021
  Annual Action Plan and throughout the 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan. Comments and
  insight from the audience will be considered as the City prepares its program plans.

  The 30-day review period will begin on or before July 10, 2020 and conclude August 10,
  2020.
   Recommended Action
  Direct staff to include all comments received for consideration in the draft of the 2020-2024
  Consolidated Plan and the 2020-2021 Annual Action Plan, recommend approval to the City
  Council, start the 30-day review, and move the plans forward to the public hearing of the
  City Council.

5. COMMENTS FROM THE AUDIENCE
  Discussion from the public of any item not specified on the agenda. Comments must pertain
  to the business of the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee. Public comments pertaining to
  the HCDA Committee’s business are welcome. Kindly limit all oral communications to five
  (5) minutes. Please complete the blue speaker card prior to the meeting and submit it to the
  Committee’s secretary.

6. COMMENTS AND CONCERNS FROM THE COMMITTEE
  Discussion from the Committee Members of any item(s) not specified on the agenda. Items
  discussed must pertain to the business of the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee.

7. ADJOURNMENT

 Copies of the staff report or other written documentation relating to each item of business described herein
 above are on file in the office of Management Services, Alhambra City Hall, 111 S. First Street, Alhambra,
 CA, and are available for public inspection during regular office hours: 7:00 A.M. to 5:30 P.M., Monday
 through Thursday.
 Should any person have a question concerning any of the above agenda items prior to the meeting described
 herein, he or she may contact Mr. Matthew Cuevas, Management Analyst, either in person, at the
 Management Services Department located at City Hall, or call via telephone at (626) 570-5011, during
 regular business hours.

 Americans with Disabilities Act: If you require special assistance to participate in any City meeting, please
 contact the City Clerk's Office (626) 570-5090. Notification of at least 72 hours prior to the meeting will
 enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to ensure accessibility to this meeting.

2.  MINUTES
  The Committee reviewed the minutes for the Regular Meeting of January 7, 2020.

  Committee Action:
  Committee Member Cosci moved, seconded by Committee Member Sharma-Ngan to
  approve the minutes of January 7, 2020.
  Ayes:  Vallejos, Cosci, Sharma-Ngan, Giese, Conchita Bañuelos.
  Noes:  None.

3. PROGRESS REPORTS
  None.

4. WORKING MEETING IN PREPARATION OF THE 2020-2024 CONSOLIDATED
  PLAN AND 2020-21 ANNUAL ACTION PLAN (CONTINUED)
  Assistant City Manager Garcia provided a brief presentation that outlined what was discussed
  at the prior meeting, and the comments and concerns expressed by Committee Members
  regarding the City of Alhambra’s CDBG and HOME programs. Assistant City Manager
  Garcia also provided an additional overview of the federal guidelines pertaining to both the
  CDBG and HOME programs. Assistant City Manager then introduced Director of Parks and

 Recreation Michael Macias.

Director Macias provided a presentation on the programs provided by the Parks and
Recreation Department that utilize CDBG funding, in particular the Case Management and
Senior Services program. Director Macias also spoke about the various youth recreation
activities the department already offers as part of its regular programming through the
General Fund and user fees. Director Macias also spoke about the City’s various parks and
the prior CDBG funds that were used to modernize and upgrade the facilities. Director
Macias explained that these programs and facilities are already funded through other funding
sources outside of the federal CDBG grant. He reiterated that the only program which
currently uses CDBG funding is the Case Management and Senior Services program, and
that any reduction to the current funding levels would have a significant impact on the
current seniors who are served by the program.

Committee Chair Vallejos inquired about the percent of HUD funds received and amounts
planned for future spending.

City Manager Binnquist answered approximately $146,000 for Case Management and the
remainder of the programs are funded by the General Fund. City Manager Binnquist further
explained that City departments and programs do not run on a cost recovery basis and are
always planned to maintain current service levels. City Manager Binnquist also explained
that the facility improvements at the parks were done with one-time funds as a result of the
dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies. She stated that since those funds are no longer
available any future park facility improvements would be done through the City’s annual
budget process as part of Capital Improvement Projects.

Committee Member Tousignant inquired about the number of individuals served and
potential duplicates pertaining to Case Management.

Director Macias replied he can provide more specific numbers.

Committee Member Bañuelos asked about upgrades to Moor Field and the surrounding track.

City Manager Binnquist replied that Moor Field is owned by the Alhambra Unified School
District and not the City; however, there is a joint-use agreement between the two entities
that allows the field to be opened to public during certain hours. City Manager further
clarified that any future upgrades would need to be done by the school district.

Committee Member Bañuelos inquired about possible future CDBG funds to upgrade
Granada Park.

City Manager Binnquist and Director Macias both replied that future funds would come from
Measure A funding and not CDBG monies. They also explained that some of the parks in the
City were not eligible for CDBG funding due to the fact they are outside of the target areas
due to the census blocks they are located in.

Committee Member Bañuelos asked when and how often the census blocks reset.

City Manager Binnquist answered that census blocks are determined through the American
Community Survey which utilizes sampling to determine income levels, and when that

  Page 2 of 6
 sampling is conducted it change the target area. City Manager Binnquist also elaborated that
much of the one-time funds used to upgrade park facilities was due to a one-time 30 percent
revenue windfall when the City sold the Alhambra Center property as a result of the
dissolution of Redevelopment Agencies throughout the state.

Police Chief Vu provided a presentation on the various crime prevention programs offered by
the Police Department which are already provided through the City’s General Fund. These
programs include a Community Academy, Vacation House Check, Volunteers on Patrol,
Police Explorer, G.R.E.A.T. Program, Youth Academy, Opportunity Academy, Night Out
Against Crime, Neighborhood Watch, and YMCA Resident Summer Camp.

The Committee thanked Chief Vu for his presentation and noted it helped to answer many of
their outstanding questions on security issues and provided them with a better understating of
what the Police Department offers.

City Manager Binnquist then provided a brief overview of the prior CDGB funds that were
used for streets and street lighting. City Manager Binnquist explained that was a result of the
sale of Fremont Plaza and the proceeds from that sale were divided among streets and alleys,
park facilities, and ADA improvements. These types of projects are not regularly budgeted
by CDBG funds due to other funding sources such as the street lighting and landscape
assessment districts.

Director of Community Deployment Marc Castagnola provided his presentation on the City’s
Housing Division. The presentation gave an overview of the department’s Minor and Major
Housing Rehabilitation programs, and the First Time Homebuyer Down Payment Assistance
program of City-owned property.

The Committee asked questions regarding the number of projects the City currently has,
guidelines for the program, and the amount of HUD funds allocated in prior and current year
for the First Time Homebuyer program.

City Manager Binnquist and Director Castagnola answered the program currently has one
project because of the time it takes to save funds to acquire and remodel property,
additionally that prospective buyers are subject to strict income eligibility requirements, and
how the current HUD funds for the HOME program are allocated and the maximum subsidy
limits. City Manager Binnquist also stated that the funding amounts are determined at the
federal level.

Committee Chair Vallejos stated he did not see the justification for maintaining the First
Time Homebuyer program given the dismal statistical numbers.

Director Castagnola felt the First Time Homebuyer program was a success and cited the 11
families that applied this past year but the department was only able to help one family due to
the funding level.

Committee Member Bañuelos asked what the current, future plans are for the program given
the expensive housing market in Alhambra.

Director Castagnola answered the City has already identified several unused lots that it plans
to develop over the next few years.

  Page 3 of 6
   Housing Assistant Holly Chenh also spoke about the families who recently obtained
  assistance with financing for a house through the program. City Manager Binnquist
  suggested possibly expanding the down payment assistance program up to $75,000. City
  Manager Binnquist also explained the difference between the rehabilitation programs and the
  acquisition program.

  Committee Member Tousignant stated he would like to see more HOME funds dedicated to
  rental needs and possible renter assistance, and possibly creating affordable housing
  developments.

  City Manager Binnquist spoke about the different programs being implemented at the
  regional level to a help renters who are struggling, and the City does not have the necessary
  funding to buy and develop large apartment building projects. City Manager Binnquist also
  stated that it was prior City Council policy to stabilize individuals into long-term housing and
  not rentals.

  Committee Member Ortiz stated if the First Time Home Buyer program is not able to cover
  staffing costs, doesn’t necessarily see the benefit and is not entirely sure if it is successful.

  Committee Chair Vallejos recessed the meeting for a short break at 8:23 p.m. Committee
  Chair Vallejos reconvened the meeting at 8:27 p.m.

5. COMMENTS FROM THE AUDIENCE
  Committee Chair Vallejos opened the meeting for comments from the audience. Seeing none,
  the comments from the audience portion of the meeting was closed.

4. WORKING MEETING IN PREPARATION OF THE 2020-2024 CONSOLIDATED
  PLAN AND 2020-21 ANNUAL ACTION PLAN (CONTINUED)
  Assistant City Manager Garcia continued the presentation on the current funding levels for
  Alhambra’s CDBG and HOME programs, and presented the Committee with various options
  for future funding allocations.

  The Committee began a discussion regarding the First Time Homebuyer program and
  whether the program should continue, and if the funds could be better used for other program
  areas or carried over to future years.

  Committee Member Cosci felt that the First Time Homebuyer program was not helping
  many people and felt those funds would be better spent in other program areas.

  Committee Member Ortiz inquired about rolling over funds from prior years and how that
  process works.

  City Manager Binnquist informed the Committee that any changes to funding allocations or
  rollovers would need to be brought back to the Committee via an amendment process, and
  subject to final approval by the City Council.

  Committee Chair Vallejos inquired about the 20 percent cap for administrative functions in
  regards to CDBG grant funds.

  Page 4 of 6
 Assistant City Manager Garcia answered they are for staffing and the importance of that
amount to ensure the City remains compliant with federal regulations.

Code Enforcement Supervisor Rafael Perez provided a brief presentation on the
responsibilities of the Code Enforcement Division and how it provides assistance to residents
through voluntary compliance and not citations.

The Committee continued its discussion on future CDBG and HOME program funding
allocations. Committee Member Tousignant inquired about the Fair Housing allocation
amounts and Committee Member Cosci asked if that amount could be reduced. City Manager
Binnquist and Director Castagnola provided answers on the amount of funding for Fair
Housing as well as additional background on the program.

There was consensus among the Committee to recommend maintaining the current funding
levels for Senior Services Case Management and Administration portions of the City’s
CDBG grant funds.

Committee Chair Vallejos asked the Committee if there was consensus to recommend
eliminating the First Time Homebuyer program.

Committee Member Bañuelos suggested reducing the current funding allocations for the
Housing Rehabilitation Minor Improvements program to $300,000 and increasing the
funding levels for Code Enforcement by $159,137 for a total of $336,137. There was
discussion among the Committee regarding the proposed funding allocations for Housing
Rehabilitation Minor Improvements and Code Enforcement as part of the City’s CDBG grant
funds. Committee Member Ortiz, Committee Member Cosci, and Committee Member
Tousignant were in favor of Committee Member Bañuelos proposal.

The Committee also inquired about possible other uses for the HOME funds regarding
Housing Rehabilitation Major Improvements and Construction, Acquisition or Rehabilitation
(CHDO).

City staff answered the Committee’s questions regarding possible other uses for these
program funds.

Committee Chair Vallejos suggested moving funding from the HOME program’s
Construction, Acquisition or Rehabilitation (CHDO) to the Housing Rehabilitation Major
Improvements portion. Committee Member Tousignant was in favor of increasing the
funding for the HOME program’s Construction, Acquisition or Rehabilitation (CHDO).

Committee Member Bañuelos stated she did not want to see the entire First Time Homebuyer
program eliminated and wanted to maintain some funding for the program.

The Committee was opposed to maintaining a minimum level of funding for the First Time
Homebuyer program and agreed to eliminate funding for the program.

Committee Member Tousignant proposed splitting future HOME funding allocations
between Construction, Acquisition or Rehabilitation (CHDO) and Housing Rehabilitation
Major Improvements. Committee Member Giese suggested a 50/50 split between the two
program areas. Committee Member Tousignant, Committee Member Ortiz, Committee

  Page 5 of 6
   Member Giese, and Committee Member Sharma-Ngan voted yes for the proposal.

  Committee Action:
  The Committee recommended maintaining the current funding levels for Senior Services
  Case Management and Administration portions of the City’s CDBG grant funds, and
  increase funding levels for Code Enforcement by $159,137 and reduce the amount for
  Housing Rehabilitation Minor Improvements to $300,000.

  The Committee recommended eliminating the First Time Homebuyer Down Payment
  Assistance program and increase funding for Construction, Acquisition or Rehabilitation
  (CHDO) by $39,000, and Housing Rehabilitation Major Improvements by $39,000.

6. COMMENTS AND CONCERNS FROM THE COMMITTEE
  None.

7. ADJOURNMENT: Committee Chair Vallejos adjourned the meeting at 9:13 p.m. to the
  Tuesday, March 3, 2020, Regular Meeting of the HCDA.

 Executive Summary
ES-05 Executive Summary - 24 CFR 91.200(c), 91.220(b)
1.  Introduction
Located in the San Gabriel Valley, Alhambra is a densely developed urban community encompassing
7.6 square miles. The City is known as the “Gateway to the San Gabriel Valley.” The San Gabriel
Valley was one of the fastest growing regions in Los Angeles County during the last part of the
twentieth century. According to the State Department of Finance, the City had a population of
86,931 persons as of January 2019. Minorities (predominantly Asians and Hispanics) are the majority
in Alhambra, comprising almost 90 percent of the population. Approximately 54 percent of the
City’s households earned 80 percent or less of the County Area Median Income (AMI).
This document constitutes the City of Alhambra's Five-Year Consolidated Plan for the use of
Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) and HOME Investment Partnership Act (HOME)
funds. The Consolidated Plan has the following major components:

    An assessment of housing and community development needs based on demographic and
  housing market information.
    Implementing strategies to address housing and community development needs.
    The Annual Action Plan outlines the City's intended uses of CDBG and HOME funds for
  the upcoming fiscal year.
This Consolidated Plan was prepared using the eConPlanning Suite system developed by the U.S.
Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). The system prescribes the structure and
contents of this document, following HUD's Consolidated Planning regulations.

2.  Summary of the objectives and outcomes identified in the Plan Needs Assessment
  Overview
The City of Alhambra has extensive housing and community development needs. CDBG and
HOME funds alone are not adequate to address the myriad of needs identified in the Needs
Assessment and Market Analysis of this Consolidated Plan. Recognizing the national objectives of
the CDBG and HOME programs and specific program regulations, the City intends to use CDBG
and HOME funds to coordinate programs, services, and projects to create a decent and suitable
living environment to benefit low and moderate income households and those with special
needs. Use of CDBG and HOME funds will focus on some of the most critical needs in Alhambra,
based on the following goals and priority needs:
Goal: Provide Decent and Affordable Housing

    High Priority: Conserve and Improve Existing Affordable Housing
    High Priority: Support Housing Code Enforcement Services
    High Priority: Support Affordable Housing Opportunities
    High Priority: Promote Equal Housing Opportunity

  first-time homebuyer using HOME funds.
    Assisted close to 1,600 persons with fair housing services.

    Completed street improvements in Low and Moderate Income Target Area.
    Provided code enforcement services to 2,650 properties in the Low and Moderate Income
  Target Area.
    Assisted over 600 seniors with case management services.

4.  Summary of citizen participation process and consultation process
The City has established the HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee with the charge of making
recommendations to the City Council regarding the use of HUD funds and the administration of the
CDBG and HOME programs.
On December 9, 2019, the City conducted a meeting before the City Council, inviting the HCDA
members to discuss priorities and potential uses for CDBG and HOME funds for the next five
years. The Council further directed staff to conduct additional meetings with the HCDA to discuss
priorities and explore other uses for the funds.
On January 7 and January 30, 2020, staff conducted additional meetings with the HCDA. The
January 7, 2020 meeting was publicly noticed and special invitations were sent to 112 agencies and
organizations that serve the low- and moderate-income persons and those with special needs in
Alhambra specifically or in the San Gabriel Valley. Neighboring cities were also invited to comment
on the region’s housing and community development needs. The list of invited agencies is included

NA-10 Housing Needs Assessment - 24 CFR 91.205 (a,b,c)
Summary of Housing Needs
As defined by HUD in the Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy (CHAS) data, housing
problems include:

    Units with physical defects (lacking complete kitchen or bathroom);
    Overcrowded conditions (housing units with more than one person per room);
    Housing cost burden (including utilities) exceeding 30 percent of gross income; and
    Severe housing cost burden (including utilities) exceeding 50 percent of gross income.
There is a need for affordable housing in Alhambra. Housing problems in the City impact renter-
households slightly more significantly, with 48 percent of all renter-households experiencing at least
one housing problem (inadequate housing, overcrowding, cost burden of 50 percent, or cost burden
of 30 percent), compared to 38 percent of owner-households (Table 8). Of the housing problems
described above, the most common was housing cost burden (Table 7).
The extent of overcrowding in the City varies by tenure, income level, and household type. About
nine percent of the City households were overcrowded and approximately 16 percent of the
overcrowded were comprised of multiple, unrelated families living together in the same home (Table
11). This may indicate that multiple families need to pool their resources in order to afford
housing. However, the majority of overcrowding occurred when large families are not able to afford
adequately sized housing.
The quality of the housing stock in the City, which includes age and the condition of the structure,
could also present potential challenges for low and moderate income households. Approximately 77
percent of housing stock, regardless of tenure, is at least 30 years old (built before 1980) and
potentially in need of rehabilitation (see Table 33 later). Many low and moderate income

Describe the number and type of single person households in need of housing assistance.

According to the 2013-2017 ACS, approximately 23 percent of households in the City were single
person households. The majority of single person households were renters (65 percent), while 35
percent were homeowners. A large proportion of single-person homeowner-households were
seniors (48 percent). ACS data indicates that approximately 15 percent of the population living alone
in the City had incomes below the poverty level.

victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault and stalking.

Persons with Disabilities: According to the 2013-2017 ACS, about nine percent of the City’s
population was affected by one or more disabilities. Among persons living with disabilities in the
City, ambulatory disabilities were the most prevalent (54 percent), followed by independent living
disabilities and cognitive disabilities (49 and 33 percent each).
As reported by the State Department of Developmental Services, as of September 2019, at least 544
Alhambra residents with developmental disabilities were being assisted by the Eastern Los Angeles
Regional Center. Most of these individuals were residing in a private home with their parent or
guardian and about 300 of these persons with developmental disabilities were under the age of 18.

What are the most common housing problems?

As mentioned previously, the most common housing problem in the City is housing cost burden.
Among the City’s renter-households, about 71 percent of all housing problems were related to
housing cost burden. Furthermore, approximately 84 percent of housing problems documented
among the City’s owner-households were related to cost burden. In comparison, units with physical
defects, or substandard units, were the least common housing problem for both City renters and
homeowners.

Are any populations/household types more affected than others by these problems?

Overall, renter-households are more impacted by housing cost burden issues than owner-
households. Approximately 71 percent of households affected by housing cost burden were renter-
households while only 29 percent were owner-households. Small households (with four or fewer
members) and elderly households in the City were also more likely than other household types to
experience a housing cost burden. Small and elderly households comprised 44 percent and 28
percent of the total low and moderate income households overpaying for housing, respectively.

Describe the characteristics and needs of Low-income individuals and families with
children (especially extremely low-income) who are currently housed but are at imminent
risk of either residing in shelters or becoming unsheltered 91.205(c)/91.305(c)). Also discuss
the needs of formerly homeless families and individuals who are receiving rapid re-housing
assistance and are nearing the termination of that assistance

Lower income families, especially those earning extremely low incomes (30 percent of Area Median
Income, or AMI), can be considered to be “at risk” of becoming homeless. These families are living
below the poverty line and are often experiencing a housing cost burden (i.e. paying more than 30
percent of their income for housing). Upon loss of employment or public assistance, these
households would likely lose their housing and end up residing in shelters or becoming homeless.
In Alhambra, approximately 21 percent (5,995 households) of households earned extremely low
incomes. Of these, 78 percent are renters and 22 percent are owners. The majority of these
households were experiencing a housing cost burden in 2015; 77 percent of extremely low income
renters and 79 percent of extremely low-income owners were paying more than 30 percent of their
income on housing.
Other persons considered at-risk for becoming homeless include victims of domestic violence,
persons with HIV/AIDS, youth recently released from foster care, and parolees. This is primarily
due to the lack of access to permanent housing and the absence of an adequate support network.
Those being released from penal, mental, or substance abuse facilities often require social services in
addition to housing assistance to help them make the transition back into society and remain off the
streets. The City contracts with the Union Station Homeless Services to provide a homeless
outreach and rapid re-housing program.
In addition, there may also be “precariously housed” persons in the City. LAHSA defines
precariously housed as a person who is staying with the household because he or she has no other

Negative Effects of Public Policies on Affordable Housing and Residential Investment
Lack of Affordable Housing Funds: The redevelopment housing set-aside fund was a significant
resource to the City of Alhambra, providing funding for homebuyer assistance, as well as new

Environmental Protection: State law (California Environmental Quality Act and California
Endangered Species Act) and federal law (National Environmental Policy Act and Federal
Endangered Species Act) regulations require environmental review of proposed discretionary
projects (e.g., subdivision maps, use permits, etc.). Costs and time delay resulting from the
environmental review process are also added to the cost of housing.
Planning and Development Fees: Planning and development impact fees, such as for
transportation, water, and sewer infrastructure improvements, often add to the overall cost of
development.
Permit and Processing Procedures: Builders and developers frequently cite the cost of holding
land during the evaluation and review process as a significant factor in the cost of
housing. Processing times vary with the complexity of the project.
State and Federal Davis-Bacon Prevailing Wages: The State Department of Industrial Relations
(DIR) expanded the kinds of projects that require the payment of prevailing wages. Prevailing wage
adds to the overall cost of development. A prevailing wage must also be paid to laborers when
federal funds are used to pay labor costs for any project over $2,000 or on any multi-family project
over eight units. Based on discussions with developers, various prevailing wage requirements
typically inflate the development costs by 35 percent.

SP-55 Barriers to affordable housing – 91.215(h)
Barriers to Affordable Housing
Lack of Affordable Housing Funds: The redevelopment housing set-aside fund was a significant
resource to the City of Alhambra, providing funding for homebuyer assistance, as well as new
construction and acquisition/rehabilitation of affordable housing. With the dissolution of
redevelopment agencies in California, the City’s ability to provide affordable housing in the
community is seriously compromised.
Environmental Protection: State law (California Environmental Quality Act and California
Endangered Species Act) and federal law (National Environmental Policy Act and Federal
Endangered Species Act) regulations require environmental review of proposed discretionary
projects (e.g., subdivision maps, use permits, etc.). Costs and time delay resulting from the
environmental review process are also added to the cost of housing.
Planning and Development Fees: Planning and development impact fees, such as for
transportation, water, and sewer infrastructure improvements, often add to the overall cost of
development.
Permit and Processing Procedures: Builders and developers frequently cite the cost of holding
land during the evaluation and review process as a significant factor in the cost of
housing. Processing times vary with the complexity of the project.
State and Federal Davis-Bacon Prevailing Wages: The State Department of Industrial Relations
(DIR) expanded the kinds of projects that require the payment of prevailing wages. Prevailing wage
adds to the overall cost of development. A prevailing wage must also be paid to laborers when
federal funds are used to pay labor costs for any project over $2,000 or on any multi-family project

Strategy to Remove or Ameliorate the Barriers to Affordable Housing
Market and governmental factors pose constraints to the provision of adequate and affordable
housing. These factors tend to disproportionately impact lower and moderate income households
due to their limited resources for absorbing the costs. Alhambra works to remove barriers to
affordable housing by implementing a Housing Element that is consistent with California law and
taking actions to reduce costs or provide off-setting financial incentives to assist in the production
of safe, high-quality, affordable housing.
Housing Element Compliance: Alhambra maintains a Housing Element as part of its state-
required General Plan. The Housing Element provides estimates of current and anticipated housing
needs, taking into account the anticipated growth of the region, for existing and future residents,
including low and moderate income households. A key component of the Housing Element is a
review of the extent to which government policies act as barriers to housing development (and
especially affordable housing development) and the jurisdiction’s commitment to eliminating or
mitigating the barriers. Pursuant to the 2013-2021 Housing Element, the City amended its Zoning
Ordinance to address the provision of emergency shelters, transitional housing, and supportive
housing. The City will be updating its Housing Element in 2020 for the 2021-2029 planning period.
The new Housing Element will focus on expanding housing opportunities.
“One-Stop” Streamline Permit Process: The Planning and Building Departments have
streamlined the permit process to provide contractors and homeowners with an easy step-by-step
guide to the permit process. On large-scale projects, City staff conducts pre-construction
coordination meetings with project proponents and all City staff who will play a role in the
construction process to help ensure a smooth running project.
Density Bonuses: Pursuant to California law, the City offers density bonuses of between 20 and 35
percent for the provision of affordable housing, depending on the amount and type of housing
provided. Financial incentives or regulatory concessions may also be granted when a developer
proposes to construct affordable housing. New State law also requires increased density up to 80

The City of Alhambra has access to Federal and local resources to achieve its housing and community development priorities. Specific

Introduction
The City takes a regional approach to homelessness. The relatively small need in the City does not
justify designing a program specifically for the homeless. Rather, through cooperative relationships
with nonprofit organizations, such as the Housing Rights Center (HRC), the Los Angeles Homeless
Service Authority (LAHSA), and the Greater Pasadena Housing and Homeless Network, the City
provides referrals and assistance to homeless individuals. The City is currently requesting proposals
for a new contract to provide homeless support services and case management, including shelter
assistance over the 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan period.

Describe the jurisdictions one-year goals and actions for reducing and ending homelessness
including reaching out to homeless persons (especially unsheltered persons) and assessing
their individual needs

The City of Alhambra is part of the Los Angeles County Continuum of Care system, participating in
regional efforts to address the need for homeless services and facilities. Homeless needs and
priorities continue to be identified through the County’s Continuum of Care System. The most
immediate needs of the homeless are emergency food, clothing, and shelter. The more long-term
needs are transitional housing, permanent housing, and supportive services in mental health, health,
employment, and transportation. The housing related needs of homeless families, while smaller in
number than the individual homeless population, are more complex than those for homeless
individuals. Larger shelter units, child care, pediatric care, and education are needed to provide a
complete system of care for homeless families.
According to LAHSA’s Point-in-Time Homeless Count in 2019, Alhambra had a very small
homeless population, estimated at 68 persons (53 unsheltered and 15 sheltered). The Alhambra
Police Department is familiar with the homeless population in the City and maintains a resource
directory for referring homeless persons in need of assistance. Specifically, the Alhambra Police
Department has a full-time 40-hour a week mental health clinician (from the County Mental Health
Services Department) who rides along in the field with a corporal. The clinician works with the
homeless to place them in psychiatric facilities, help locate their families, reunite them with family,
reserve them space at shelters, and connect them with service providers, etc. The clinician assists
with any other mental health issues in the schools, domestic calls, etc. The City will continue to
partner with the County Mental Health Services Department to assist the homeless in obtaining
more permanent housing arrangements and other supportive services

Addressing the emergency shelter and transitional housing needs of homeless persons
Homeless prevention services are also available citywide through the Fair Housing program
provided by the Housing Rights Center. Fair housing services assist those who are at risk of
becoming homeless by improving the tenant/landlord relationship, reducing evictions, and assisting
households in finding adequate housing. The City's senior case management program also assists
many seniors with extremely low incomes and allowing them to continue to age in place. Other
homeless services and facilities are provided by agencies located throughout the San Gabriel Valley
that help prevent homelessness.

Introduction
Market and governmental factors pose constraints to the provision of adequate and affordable
housing. These factors tend to disproportionately impact lower and moderate income households
due to their limited resources for absorbing the costs. Alhambra works to remove barriers to
affordable housing by implementing a Housing Element that is consistent with California law and
taking actions to reduce costs or provide off-setting financial incentives to assist in the production
of safe, high-quality, affordable housing. The City is committed to removing governmental
constraints that hinder the production of housing, and offers a “one-stop” streamlined permitting
process to facilitate efficient entitlement and building permit processing.

Actions it planned to remove or ameliorate the negative effects of public policies that serve
as barriers to affordable housing such as land use controls, tax policies affecting land,
zoning ordinances, building codes, fees and charges, growth limitations, and policies
affecting the return on residential investment

Housing Element Compliance: Alhambra maintains a Housing Element as part of its state-
required General Plan. The Housing Element provides estimates of current and anticipated housing
needs, taking into account the anticipated growth of the region, for existing and future residents,
including low and moderate income households. A key component of the Housing Element is a
review of the extent to which government policies act as barriers to housing development (and
especially affordable housing development) and the jurisdiction’s commitment to eliminating or
mitigating the barriers. Pursuant to the 2013-2021 Housing Element, the City amended its Zoning
Ordinance to address the provision of emergency shelters, transitional housing, and supportive
housing. The City will be updating its Housing Element in 2020 for the 2021-2029 planning period.
The new Housing Element will focus on expanding housing production.
“One-Stop” Streamline Permit Process: The Planning and Building Departments have
streamlined the permit process to provide contractors and homeowners with an easy step-by-step
guide to the permit process. On large-scale projects, City staff conducts pre-construction
coordination meetings with project proponents and all City staff who will play a role in the
construction process to help ensure a smooth running project.
Density Bonuses: Pursuant to California law, the City offers density bonuses of between 20 and 35
percent for the provision of affordable housing, depending on the amount and type of housing
provided. Financial incentives or regulatory concessions may also be granted when a developer
proposes to construct affordable housing. New State law also requires a density bonus of up to 80
percent for 100 percent affordable projects

Introduction
This section discusses the City's underserved needs and institutional structure for delivering housing
and community development activities.

Actions planned to address obstacles to meeting underserved needs
The City's underserved populations include the elderly, disabled, and low and moderate income
households. The City will rely on its existing network of public and nonprofit service agencies, along
with the City's Joslyn Senior Center, to provide an array of supportive services for the City's
underserved groups. In addition, the City will use CDBG funds to support the fair housing program
that targets many of the City's underserved residents. Fair housing is a homeless prevention strategy,
allowing many equal access to housing and assisting those facing unfair treatment in the housing
market. As funding permits, CDBG funds may also be used to fund ADA improvements at public
facilities, benefitting persons with disabilities that are often underserved.

Actions planned to foster and maintain affordable housing

The City will continue to foster affordable housing development in the community through
incentives such as density bonuses for affordable housing, mixed use development, and lot
consolidation. In addition, fair housing as a homeless prevention strategy can assist those facing
unfair evictions and foreclosure frauds, and therefore be able to remain at their homes.

Actions planned to reduce lead-based paint hazards

Lead-based paint abatement is fully integrated into the City's Housing Rehabilitation Program
The City's Code Enforcement staff will continue to provide information of lead-based paint hazards
and resources for abatement to residents. Such information is also available at public counters.

Actions planned to reduce the number of poverty-level families

The City seeks to reduce the number of people living in poverty (extremely low-income households
earning less than 30 percent of the AMI) by continuing to implement a number of programs,
including housing assistance, case management services for seniors, and economic development
activities. As a means of reducing the number of persons with incomes below the poverty line, the
City will coordinate its efforts with those of other public and private organizations providing
economic development and job training programs.

Actions planned to develop institutional structure
City staff will continue to consult with HUD staff and attend HUD trainings in order to better craft
the CDBG and HOME programs that can be delivered in a cost-effective manner.

Annually, the City receives allocations from HUD for the CDBG and HOME programs. The City
does not have an official application process to distribute these funds for housing and community
development programs and activities. Every January/February, the City conducts a public hearing
with the HCDA to assess housing and community development needs. Individuals/organizations
are encouraged to provide input and submit a written request for funding. HCDA would review the
request and determine if funding allocations/priorities should be adjusted to accommodate the
request.

The City offers a Housing Rehabilitation Program to low and moderate income households. The
City advertises at all city counters for the programs, on the City website, and in Around Alhambra
for special advertising when funding is available. The City accepts the applications on a first-come-
first-serve basis, unless there is a case of urgent need, which then is prioritized for funding and
processing. An urgent need case refers to an unsafe (i.e. failing roof) or uninhabitable (i.e. no heat,

  Minutes of the City of Alhambra’s
  HCDA Citizen Advisory Committee
  Special Meeting of June 16, 2020
  MEETING CONDUCTED VIA TELECONFERENCE/ZOOM DUE TO COVID-19.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia called the meeting to order at 7:03 p.m.

1. ROLL CALL:
  Committee Members Present:
  Bill Vallejos, Chair*  Mark Lee, Vice Chair
  Maria Conchita Bañuelos  Andrea Giese
  Marc Tousignant  Bonita Sharma-Ngan
  Sasha Renée Pérez  Yvette Cardenas

  *Committee Chair Vallejos joined the meeting at 7:22 p.m.

  Committee Members Absent:
  Marcos Sayon

  City Staff Present:
  Lucy Garcia, Assistant City Manager
  Veronica Tam, Veronica Tam and Associates
  Matthew Cuevas, Management Analyst

  New HCDA Committee Member, Yvette Cardenas, was introduced by Assistant City
  Manager Garcia.

2. MINUTES
  The Committee reviewed the minutes for the Special Meeting of January 30, 2020.

  Committee Action:
  Vice Chair Lee moved, seconded by Committee Member Bañuelos, to approve the minutes
  for the special meeting of January 30, 2020.
  Ayes:  Lee, Sharma-Ngan, Bañuelos, Giese, Tousignant, Pérez and Cardenas.
  Noes:  None.
  Abstain: None.

3. PROGRESS REPORTS
  The Committee reviewed the reports. All figures indicate the progress made and services
  rendered to date for FY 2019-2020. Assistant City Manager Garcia gave an overview of the
  current progress reports, including the additional COVID-19 funding under CDBG the City
  received for COVID-19 testing and for a housing assistance program for 200 low- and
  moderate-income households to provide $500 a month for rental/mortgage assistance
  payments for three months.

  Committee Member Pérez inquired how many applications were received for the housing
  assistance program, how applicants were notified if they were selected, and any households
  that may have include undocumented individuals.

  Page 1 of 5
   Assistant City Manager Garcia answered the City received approximately 2,000 applications,
  and City staff has been processing applications as quickly as possible but faced challenges
  collecting required documentation. In addition, applicants also need to provide proper
  identification, income status, and permanent resident or citizenship, per HUD requirements,
  in order to be eligible for funding. Assistant City Manager Garcia also added that
  approximately 70 to 75 applicants had been approved to date.

  Committee Member Cardenas asked about the COVID-19 testing aspect moving from
  symptomatic individuals to including all Alhambra residents, and other uses the CDBG funds
  could be used for. Citing one in the city of El Monte for assistance to local small businesses
  in the form of loans up to $10,000.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia replied the City tested 1,599 individuals and ultimately
  included asymptomatic individuals due to the health department encouraging the testing of
  these individuals since they could still spread the virus unknowingly. Assistant City Manager
  also replied the City received a list from HUD for eligible COVID related activities and it left
  each jurisdiction discretion on how to apply those funds and those were the concepts that
  unfolded and approved by City Council.

  Committee Member Pérez asked if the City was going to be receiving any additional CDBG
  funds.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia replied at this time the City does not anticipate any additional
  CDBG funding but ultimately it would be up to Congress and the President.

  Committee Action:
  The Committee received and filed these informational reports.

4. DRAFT 2020-2024 CONSOLIDATED PLAN AND 2020-2021 ANNUAL ACTION
  PLAN
  Assistant City Manager Garcia introduced Veronica Tam to provide the presentation on the
  draft 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan and the 2020-2021 Annual Action Plan.

  Ms. Tam opened her presentation by sharing the list of eligible activities, provided by HUD,
  regarding the CDBG COVID-19 funding to the Committee, and outlined some of the
  challenges of setting up these activities without violating HUD policies. One challenge was
  ensuring that jurisdictions were not providing a duplication of benefits under HUD policies.
  Ms. Tam also touched on potential phase two funding but indicated that typically goes to
  communities with high homeless populations.

  Assistant City Manager Garcia spoke about the business assistance aspect and at the time
  many programs were being offered through the state and the county, the City wanted to
  ensure there wasn’t a duplication of benefits. Whereas the COVID-19 testing was designed
  specifically for Alhambra and the convenience factor being locally accessible to residents.

  Ms. Tam began her presentation on the 2020-2024 Consolidated Plan and 2020-2021 Annual
  Action Plan. She informed the Committee that the City has received over $1 million in
  federal funding, and CDBG funds are primarily used to eliminate blight and improve the
  quality of life for low- and moderate-income individuals. Ms. Tam also reiterated that the
  HOME funds are used for increasing and preserving affordable housing for low- and
  moderate-income households and cannot be used in any other way. Ms. Tam also noted that
  Page 2 of 5
 this is the first time over her entire career where the designation for an Urgent Need under
HUD has been authorized due to COVID-19.

Ms. Tam touched upon the revised goals and priorities the Committee agreed upon as a result
of prior HCDA meetings including:

  − Conserve and improve existing affordable housing
  − Support housing Code Enforcement Services
  − Support affordable housing opportunities
  − Promote equal housing opportunity
  − Provide needed community and supportive services, especially for Senior Services
  − Provide community facility/infrastructure improvement, especially ADA projects
  − Provide for planning and administrative activities

In her presentation Ms. Tam discussed the upcoming 2020-2021 CDBG Action Plan and
reviewed the Committee’s revised funding priorities including:

  −  $314,374 for Housing Rehabilitation
  −  $344,798 for Code Enforcement
  −  $25,000 for Fair Housing Services
  −  $152,117 for Senior Case Management Services
  −  $177,822 for Administration

Ms. Tam then reiterated the Committee’s revised funding priorities for the 2020-2021
HOME Action Plan, including:

  − $451,469 for Housing Rehabilitation
  − $146,064 for CHDO Reserve
  − $66,393 for Administration

Assistant City Manager Garcia informed the Committee that since the last meeting, the City
had received a small increase in funding from HUD.

Committee Member Tousignant inquired what the new amount was.

Assistant City Manager Garcia answered it was approximately $100,000 and the additional
funds were spread out among the various priorities the Committee had identified prior.

Committee Member Pérez asked about Code Enforcement activities in relation to affordable
housing issues and citations issued for minor violations like peeling paint or brown lawns.

Assistant City Manger Garcia and Ms. Tam answered that the CDBG portion of Code
Enforcement funding can only be used in the designated target areas throughout the City that
utilize CDBG funds, and any enforcement actions are restricted to major building code and
health and safety violations. In relation to the Code Enforcement funding, Ms. Tam also
explained at the same time the Committee increased funding for Housing Rehabilitation in
order to give property owners a chance to fix any substandard issues.

Assistant City Manager Garcia stated City staff would arrange for a future presentation from
Code Enforcement to provide the Committee with an overview of the division’s
  Page 3 of 5
   responsibilities with respect to CDBG activities.

  Committee Member Cardenas inquired about a table in the draft plan that was not displaying
  percentages or proportions and asked if those could be added into the table.

  Ms. Tam agreed with Committee Member Cardenas that the tables were challenging but
  answered unfortunately the tables could not be updated because the template is provided by
  HUD. Ms. Tam further explained that technical documentation on how to present census
  data, in conjunction with the American Community Survey data, should never be presented
  as absolute numbers since they are survey estimates.

  Committee Member Cardenas asked if the unemployment figures in the draft document can
  be updated to reflect the current numbers.

  Ms. Tam answered she would check to see if the Bureau of Labor Statistics had published
  updated numbers, and if they are available she would include those revised figures.

  Committee Member Cardenas noted there appeared to be some missing information on page
  12 of the draft document relating to table 11.

  Ms. Tam stated she would review that page and make any necessary revisions.

  Committee Member Cardenas inquired about the removal of the First Time Homebuyer
  program.

  Ms. Tam explained the reasoning why the Committee decided to eliminate that program and
  the difficulty of purchasing a home with a price that meets HUD standards.

  Committee Member Pérez asked if residents would be eligible for Los Angeles County’s
  First Time Homebuyer Program.

  Ms. Tam answered it depended on the funding source and most communities throughout the
  state do not offer this type of program, but they check with the state Housing and Community
  Development Department to look for other programs.

  Committee Member Bañuelos added there are non-profit organizations that offer down
  payment assistance and first-time homebuyer programs in Los Angeles County but depends
  upon certain qualifications.
